rv.q: Would I see it again? Duh, already planning on it.
More than anything, the show presents a message of empowerment, as we watch Cher fight for the right to control her career — and her life.
The result is a show that works far better than it has any right to do, one that manages to be simultaneously kitschy and touching.

The Cher Show is a jukebox musical that works harder than most to justify its existence, and mostly succeeds in doing so by focusing on what made Cher an icon: her ability to constantly reinvent herself.
For a musical with all the depth of a spread in Us Weekly, “The Cher Show,” running nearly 2½ hours, seems ludicrously long.
The exuberant, occasionally tacky jukebox musical that tells her life story is more faltering.
Still it succeeds as a story of one woman's persistence and survival.
The lack of creative ambition and innovation is dispiriting, especially when Jersey Boys, Beautiful and Lazarus have already proven these things needn’t be dreadful.

"Except for the dozens of eye-popping outfits Mr. Mackie gorgeously recreates for the occasion, it’s all gesture, no craft: dramatically threadbare and surprisingly unrevealing...You can’t distinguish scenes meant to borrow comedy-hour elements from those meant to be taken at face value...
Despite an icon with attitude, an armful of pop tunes and a can-do cast, the script never quite finds a satisfying style — or a genuine heart — as a winning stage musical.
Maybe the thing to do with The Cher Show is to regard it as a theater-sized tweet and a fan’s treat.
Take it from me: The Cher Show does Cher proud and the show delivers enormous entertainment in doing so.
If we are going to have to live with bio-musicals as a regular part of the Broadway season, then let The Cher Show serve as an exemplar of the form.

"The uneven book and the fabulous frocks are not all there is to this dazzling, ultimately entertaining glitz-fest. Moore’s direction is lightning-fast, giving the proceedings the speed and flash of a Vegas concert, and the performances rise above the 'Behind the Music' milieu of the story...Stephanie J.

"Perhaps the best reason to spend your money on this tuner is the chance to see Stephanie J. Block turn in a performance of a lifetime as one of three women sharing the title role. Amazingly, Block manages to sound almost identical to Cher without relying on cheesy mannerisms or outright imitation, both while singing and delivering dialogue.
Artistically, it's no match for 'Jersey Boys.' But while that show has a special appeal to men, Cher's message of facing one's fears strikes a resonant chord among women and flamboyant gentlemen.
The same can be said for The Cher Show.
But it is, in the tradition of the American jukebox musical, a fair simulation.
Thus, with a book that barely knows what it’s doing, balanced by a director, a costumer and a star who very much do, The Cher Show is easily the most exciting new Broadway musical of the season.
The one word to describe The Cher Show is glitzy.
Where Diamond and Wicks are giving fine tribute concert impersonations, Block makes the role her own and delivers the closest thing this show has to real emotional connection.
The problem isn't that it's all too much.
But it could have been a whole lot more.
Ultimately, I don’t hate The Cher Show since, despite all of the mess, it leaves you wanting to Believe!
The musical, at two and a half hours, is a mostly familiar trek through life moments shorn of revelation.
Maybe the only one who could really make Cher's story soar would be the ageless "goddess" herself.
One could argue that Cher’s fans expect no less – and no more – than what The Cher Show gives them: glitz, hits and highlights.
The Cher Show benefits from the subject's breezily candid persona, but, as an account of a tumultuous life and times, it has all the incisive detail of a photo-heavy People magazine profile.
The production proves to be more tolerable than similar star-worship vehicles, though nowhere near as satisfying as “Jersey Boys” (The Four Seasons) or even “Beautiful” (Carole King).
The jokes are lame, segues between scenes are blunt or nonexistent, and a general lack of inventiveness pervades the entire enterprise.
The Cher Show, with the astonishing Block as tour guide and hostess with the very mostest, is a show to truly “Believe” in.
The cast and creative team behind The Cher Show have brought a spectacular production to Broadway.

“The book...although a bit campy...is crystal clear and informative...’The Cher Show’ might be billed as a jukebox musical; however...her songs fit perfectly into her life story...Gattelli gives...energetic production numbers...Moore moves the evening along at a fast pace...Then there are the costumes...An endless parade of astonishing outfits...

It never tries to be anything it is not, wholly owning its own wry silliness and decadent camp while still honoring the pop legend whose story it quite legibly tells, and remaining blissfully entertaining from start to finish.
I generally enjoyed the party, even if some scenes seem inconsequential.
In short, this is a fluffy bauble that knows exactly what it is and exactly how to entertain.
For splash, sparkle, and the sensational Stephanie J. Block, The Cher Show is a good-time jukebox musical.
“The Cher Show” is a much better than anticipated show and though it isn’t groundbreaking or, at least for me, life-changing, it is an entertaining production and a must-see for Cher fans.

"There’s amazing Mackie costumes, there’s hunky backup dancers, there’s plenty of Cher-ism jokes pulled from her tweets, and there is even some feminism in there too...So focus on the rhinestones and the songs you love, and try not to to scoff at the whiplash-inducing, uneven book.
Cher the icon is campy and fun with an incredible sense of humor; more of this show should have followed that track. That it works at all is a credit to Block, who gives a truly stellar performance.
This is sensational actress-singer Block's show as she turns in a rousing performance.
THE CHER SHOW is a lot more fun than SUMMER (both suffer from weak books) because Cher is, well, Cher.
The earnestness that takes over in the second act is a bit hard to take; let’s not oversell the importance of someone best known for her spangled bat wings and furry headdresses.

And not enough love in the world (I’ll stop now) could save “The Cher Show” from its disappointingly guarded and directionless attempt to squeeze Cher’s many lives into a bordered, formulaic dramatization of her career.
I had a fantastic night and got more than my money's worth
Just go see the show, overlook the weak spots and be prepared to be dazzled.
Worst of all, it slows the show down.

cn.t: Critics give this glitzy jukebox bio-musical mixed reviews, praising Bob Mackie's dazzling costumes and Stephanie J. Block's standout performance, but faulting its shallow, TV variety show-style storytelling that rushes through Cher's life at breakneck speed.

sg.ra: For MJ the Musical's dance-heavy choreography, Center Orchestra rows A-H sit entirely in front of the mezzanine overhang (which begins at row J) and deliver head-on sightlines of the performers' feet — critical for a Michael Jackson dance biomusical. Row A seats 107-110 are frequently cited as the theatre's best, but rows C-D balance proximity with neck-angle comfort.

Because Neil Simon's orchestra is unusually deep (25 rows, A-Z) and the mezzanine overhang only starts cutting the top of the stage noticeably by row S, rows H-P give you full head-on views with no overhang effect at non-premium pricing — a specific quirk of this house's long orchestra footprint.

The mezzanine overhang is felt from row J onward and by rows S-Z it actively cuts off the top of the stage per SeatPlan's orchestra guide — a real issue for MJ the Musical, which uses tall set pieces and lifts. Unique to Neil Simon because the orchestra runs all the way to row Z, pushing rear seats deep under the overhang.

Front Center Mezzanine rows A-B give an elevated, unobstructed sweep — particularly valuable at Neil Simon because MJ the Musical uses formation choreography that reads better from above. Tripadvisor users confirm no obstruction issues at front mezz (photo cited from row A seat 103). Row A also has the best legroom in the mezzanine.

Specific Neil Simon quirk: Left and Right Mezzanine rows H and L sit directly behind railings that border the internal staircase, making legroom 'very tight' — SeatPlan calls out seats H1-7 and L9-15 by number. This is a house-specific hazard, not the generic 'Broadway legroom is tight' complaint.

Rear mezzanine at Neil Simon has a shallow rake — a specific architectural quirk noted by SeatPlan — so rows S-U feel distant and lose detail on the stage front, and the mezzanine's own underside can minor-obstruct the back-row view. For MJ's facial-expression moments in 'Man in the Mirror' numbers this is a real detriment.

Three boxes are staggered off the Left Mezzanine at Neil Simon — a specific architectural feature of this house — and SeatPlan explicitly states the viewing experience 'isn't the best' because the angle is fully side-on. Priced as premium but not worth it for a dance musical where frontal sightlines matter.
